Based on the retrieved healthcare Q&A matches, it appears that there is no clear evidence to support the presence of a "July effect" in patients undergoing major cancer surgery. The available data suggest that outcomes for patients with major cancer surgery remain relatively consistent across different time periods without any notable differences due to the month of surgery.

In fact, multiple completion notes emphasize that:

- There is an absence of a July effect in patients undergoing major cancer surgery.
- Both surgery and radiation therapy significantly improve median, 5-, and 10-year survival rates for extrapulmonary small cell cancers (EPSCC).
- Intraoperative neuromonitoring has been associated with improved functional outcomes in patients undergoing open Tumor Microdissection (TME) for rectal cancer.
- Patients with impaired fasting blood glucose levels preoperatively are at increased risk of mortality after Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG) surgery.
- There is no established benefit to aspiration thrombectomy before primary Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI) in patients with primary rectal cancer.

Therefore, based on the available evidence from these healthcare Q&A matches, there is currently no conclusive evidence to support the presence of a "July effect" in patients undergoing major cancer surgery.
